capabilities.name: Authentication & Authorization
capabilities.notes: Provides robust authentication via OIDC/OAuth2 providers and basic auth. Handles session management, token validation, and user identity extraction.

capabilities.name: Configuration Management
capabilities.notes: Supports configuration via flags and environment variables (implied by Go binary structure and options package imports). Does not support dynamic runtime policy updates or geofence definitions.

capabilities.name: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
capabilities.notes: Can extract user groups/roles from OIDC providers and forward them as headers, enabling upstream RBAC. Does not enforce access control itself.

capabilities.name: Session Management
capabilities.notes: Manages user sessions via cookies and tokens. Supports session refresh and validation.

capabilities.name: Geofencing
capabilities.notes: No evidence of geolocation or geofence capabilities in the codebase.

constraints: Requires network access to OIDC/OAuth2 identity providers
Requires TLS termination or reverse proxy setup for secure header forwarding

assumptions: Assumes existing OIDC/OAuth2 identity provider is available
Assumes upstream application can accept authentication headers
Configuration will be managed via environment variables or config files

evidence.claim: OAuth2 Proxy provides authentication with Google, Azure, OpenID Connect and many more identity providers.
Supports htpasswd-based basic authentication with SHA1 & bcrypt password hashing.
Uses gorilla/mux for HTTP routing and alice for middleware chaining.

validation.judge_notes: REVISE: [critical] The artifact claims a runtime requirement of Go 1.26+. As of the current date (and even in late 2024/early 2025), Go 1.26 does not exist. The latest stable releases are in the 1.21-1.23 range. This is a fabricated or hallucinated version number, indicating unreliable metadata. | [high] The passport marks this capability as 'verified', but the only code-level evidence provided (`oauthproxy.go`) defines URL paths (constants) and imports. It does not contain the implementation logic for OIDC/OAuth2 flows or token validation. The README is marketing text, which the rubric explicitly excludes from verifying 'verified' status. No source file implementing the actual authentication handshake is cited. | [high] The claim is supported only by `oauthproxy.go`, which defines constants and imports. There is no evidence excerpt showing the code that manages sessions (cookies, tokens, refresh logic). The session management logic resides in `pkg/sessions/` or similar, which is imported but not examined in the evidence. | [medium] The claim states it can extract user groups/roles. The evidence cited is `README.md`. While the README mentions extracting details, the rubric requires code/test evidence for verification of capabilities if possible, or at least consistent status. More importantly, the confidence is low (0.6). This is acceptable as 'inferred', but the claim that it 'enables upstream RBAC' is a functional assertion not proven by the README alone without seeing header forwarding logic in code. | [medium] The artifact claims MIT license. The evidence `LICENSE@39ec0e19` shows the standard MIT text. However, the evidence excerpt cuts off at "THE SOFTWARE IS PROVIDED "AS IS", WITH". While likely MIT, the truncation prevents full verification of the copyright holder and permission grant completeness in the provided snippet. Additionally, the metadata says `license_api=mit`. This is likely correct but the evidence snippet is incomplete.

description: OAuth2 Proxy is a reverse proxy and middleware component that provides authentication via OAuth2/OIDC providers. It intercepts HTTP requests, redirects users to an identity provider for login, validates tokens (JWT/OIDC), and forwards authenticated requests to upstream services with user claims in HTTP headers. It also supports basic authentication via htpasswd files.
deployment_constraints: Requires network access to OIDC/OAuth2 identity providers
Requires TLS termination or reverse proxy setup for secure header forwarding
known_gaps: No native MQTT support for configuration distribution
No dynamic policy engine (static configuration only)
No user role/permission management UI or API (relies on upstream)
risks: MIT License is permissive but lacks patent protection
Volunteer-driven project may have variable response times for security issues
Complex OIDC provider configurations can be error-prone
No built-in audit logging for authentication events

adaptation_assumptions: Assumes existing OIDC/OAuth2 identity provider is available
Assumes upstream application can accept authentication headers
